A vulnerability in the NX-API feature of Cisco NX-OS Software could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges or cause a denial of service (DoS) condition on an affected device. 
The vulnerability is due to insufficient input validation of data that is sent to the NX-API. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted HTTP request to the NX-API of an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges and could cause process crashes, which could result in a reload of the device and a DoS condition.

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. 
This advisory is available at the following link:

Something happened in the U.S. Treasury market that’s hard to ignore.

The quarter closed with 20-year Treasury yields at 5.68% and 30-year yields at 5.64%. These are levels the market hasn’t seen in more than 20 years. And this is no longer just a random spike lasting a couple of days, but a very noticeable shift in the cost of long-term borrowing.

Why are yields rising? Investors want an increasingly larger premium for lending money to the U.S. government for decades. The reasons are clear. Massive government debt, a large budget deficit, inflation that remains elevated, and a huge amount of new borrowing. In other words, the market is demanding an increasingly higher price for long-term U.S. debt.

And here’s the key question. What happens if 5% or 6% turn out not to be the ceiling, and yields eventually climb to 8%, 9%, or even 10%? For now, that’s not the base-case scenario, but if it happens, the rules of the game in financial markets will change dramatically.

Because when U.S. government bond yields hit 8%, investors face a simple question. Why take on significant risk in stocks, crypto, real estate, or gold when you can earn that kind of return in dollars from one of the most reliable financial instruments in the world? At that point, some capital could start flowing into Treasuries, and all other asset classes would have to offer significantly higher potential returns to remain attractive.

My takeaway is simple. Right now, it’s important to watch not just stocks and crypto, but the bond market as well. If the era of cheap money really is over, long-term Treasuries could become one of the key indicators of where global capital is headed next.

TRUMP'S EXECUTIVE ORDER ON DIESEL WILL REQUIRE U.S. DEPARTMENT LEADERS TO IDENTIFY PATHS AROUND LOCAL AND STATE REGULATIONS THAT HINDER ENERGY PRODUCTION — ACCORDING TO THREE SOURCES

Token Echo

An Ethereum Foundation researcher suggests pre-transferring large sums to addresses that have not yet signed any transactions

On October 7th, Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake called on the crypto industry to calmly prepare for a scenario in which the ECDSA signature scheme could be hacked before the advent of a quantum computer. In his estimation, in the worst case, this could be a matter of months, not years. There is no confirmed method for such a hack.

Drake described the hack as rapid recovery of a private key from an already disclosed public one: for example, in about a week with available hardware such as a large cluster of graphics processors. According to him, it is now reasonable to prepare for such a possibility. He linked the warning to recent progress in mathematical models, including the publication of a set of mathematical works by OpenAI's internal model. The main risk, according to Drake, concerns addresses that have already signed transactions and thus revealed their public key. He recommends that large and prepared holders transfer most of their funds to addresses that have not signed anything yet. After each outgoing transaction, it is also better to transfer the remainder to a new address. You don't need a new wallet for this: you can get the address from the same seed phrase.

Drake specifically asks not to rush. According to him, there is cause for action, but a hasty transfer can do more harm than good. For wallets with less than 50 bitcoins, he sees partial coverage in already disclosed Satoshi addresses: around 20 thousand addresses with 50 bitcoins each. For oracle operators and second-layer network security advisors, he recommends changing the ECDSA key after each signed message or supplementing the signature with a hash-based scheme, such as SPHINCS.

According to his estimation, one can only exit this regime with cryptography designed for the period after the current development of artificial intelligence. Drake himself leans towards hash-based schemes and moving away from cryptography that relies on elliptic curves, lattices, or isogenies. In November, he plans to discuss the topic with institutional participants at a meeting in London.
